one_liner: Pure-C# LSM-tree ordered key-value engine for .NET; beats RocksDB (via RocksDbSharp) and SQLite on its own indexed profile-store benchmark.
what_it_does: ZoneTree is an embedded, persistent, ordered key-value store for .NET. It is meant as the storage layer under custom databases, indexes, queues, event stores and time-series layers, not as a finished database. You build a generic IZoneTree<TKey,TValue> through ZoneTreeFactory with pluggable serializers and comparers, then call Upsert/TryAdd/TryDelete/TryGet, use forward and reverse seekable iterators, run atomic read-modify-write methods, or open a separate transactional tree that uses optimistic transactions. It does not implement RocksDB's API or SQL: schemas, secondary indexes and queries are the application's job.
how_it_is_fast: It is a classic LSM tree. Writes land in an in-memory B+Tree mutable segment (128-entry nodes, node-level monitor locks by default) that sits behind a concurrent Bloom filter and a background async Zstd-compressed WAL. A background maintainer then freezes these segments and merges them into sorted, compressed disk segments. Disk segments are 'multipart': each logical segment is a set of immutable key-range parts, so a merge rewrites only the parts whose range changed and carries clean parts forward, which bounds write amplification. Reads go through a sparse index (step 16 in the benchmark, 1,024 by default), a cache of decompressed 4 MB blocks, 16-entry materialized key/value chunks, per-segment circular key/value caches and prefetch hints for sequential lookups; the project attributes its higher peak memory to the decompressed-block caching.
when_to_use: .NET services that need an embedded, ordered, persistent key-value store with seek/range scans and reverse iteration, and want only managed dependencies (K4os LZ4 and ZstdSharp ports, no native RocksDB binaries). It supports NativeAOT on net7.0 and later.

Read-heavy point lookups and ordered index scans with a working set that fits in RAM with room to spare. At 2M profiles it did 970,010 id reads/s vs RocksDB's 272,133/s and 388,867 email lookups/s vs 138,471/s.
Live, unbatched single-record writes where SQLite autocommit becomes the bottleneck. At 2M profiles it inserted 182,070 rows/s vs SQLite's 6,231/s (WAL journal, synchronous=NORMAL).

Building your own index, queue, event-store, TTL or full-text layer on an ordered keyspace. There is an official ZoneTree.FullTextSearch package, plus operation indexes for async replication and live backup of non-transactional trees.
Cache, temporary or rebuildable data. The NoWAL mode removes WAL cost entirely.
when_not_to_use: Memory-constrained hosts. Peak process memory vs RocksDB was 3.3 GB vs 1.1 GB at 2M profiles, 33.0 GB vs 3.6 GB at 20M, and 56.3 GB vs 11.1 GB at 100M on a 60.4 GB machine, where ZoneTree's on-disk data was only 7.4 GB.

Write-dominated workloads at tens of millions of rows. On the project's own 20M and 50M runs, RocksDB's raw insert and update phases were faster (20M: 173,190 vs 156,633 inserts/s and 44,044 vs 39,440 updates/s). At 100M, updates were a tie. In issue #108 a user loading 10M string-to-byte[] records measured 7.8 s for ZoneTree vs 4.5 s for RocksDB with batched writes. Without batching, ZoneTree was about 4x faster, and random lookups were about even.

You need SQL, native secondary indexes, joins or cross-language access. ZoneTree is a .NET-only key-value engine, and the benchmark maintains every secondary index in application code as a separate tree.

Strict per-write power-loss durability. The default AsyncCompressed WAL can lose recent writes on a crash. Even Sync WAL only flushes to the OS kernel (maintainer, issue #116), and SyncCompressed writes its tail every 500 ms.

If you are comparing against a tuned modern RocksDB, the published numbers do not tell you the answer. The harness uses RocksDB 6.2.2 through the RocksDbSharp P/Invoke wrapper as five separate instances and sets no block-based-table options (no Bloom filter, no enlarged block cache). Meanwhile ZoneTree runs with a dense sparse index and a block cache bounded by lifetime, not size.

integration.min_toolchain: .NET 6 (multi-targets net6.0 through net10.0; library built with C# 14 / LangVersion 14.0)
integration.platforms: any .NET 6-10 runtime (managed code with unsafe blocks). Published benchmark runs are Linux x64 and Windows 11 x64.
integration.thread_safety: The regular write and read APIs (Upsert, TryAdd, TryDelete, TryGet) are designed for concurrent use. Atomic methods synchronize only with each other, for same-key read-modify-write. Multi-key atomicity needs a transactional tree with optimistic transactions. The in-memory B+Tree defaults to node-level monitor locks. NoLock mode is single-thread only.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false. It has its own generic C# API, not RocksDB's C++ API or a SQL interface, and data must be migrated. In the benchmark both engines use a similar layout (one store per index), so porting a RocksDB-style multi-store design is direct, but porting a SQLite schema means rebuilding indexes in application code.

gotchas: Values in in-memory segments are held by reference. Mutating an object after Upsert, or one returned by TryGet or ReadCommittedTryGet, silently changes what readers see: no WAL record, and a transaction rollback does not undo it (issue #120). Use immutable records or structs, or clone before upserting.

The comparer, serializers and value types are part of the database identity and cannot change behavior on an existing store. A custom comparer also needs an IKeyHasher that agrees with its equality (for example, a case-insensitive string comparer needs a case-insensitive hasher), or the mutable-segment Bloom filter can wrongly report misses.

Memory limits are record counts, not bytes: MutableSegmentMaxItemCount defaults to 1,000,000, which is far too much for large string or document values. You also need a maintainer (CreateMaintainer) or your own maintenance loop, or read-only segments pile up. .NET keeps freed memory, so process RSS stays high after merges.

In v1.8.7 the package and namespace were renamed from Tenray.ZoneTree to ZoneTree, and in v1.9.0 the repo moved from koculu/ZoneTree to the ZoneTree org. TotalRecordCount counts physical versions, not live keys (use Count()). Built-in live backup does not cover transactional trees.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ZoneTree when your code is .NET and you want an ordered, embedded, managed-only store with range scans. Most siblings here (Badger, Pogreb, SurrealKV, Speedb, ToplingDB, SplinterDB, NuDB) are Go, Rust or C/C++ engines and would need a native binding such as the RocksDbSharp wrapper this benchmark used. F2/FASTER is the other .NET-relevant sibling; the ZoneTree repo ships a ZoneTree-vs-FASTER harness for Int64 point inserts and lookups but publishes no results from it, so that head-to-head is unmeasured.
verified_claims_summary: On the project's own 2M-profile run (one worker, .NET 10.0.9 Release with Server GC, AMD EPYC 4345P 8C/16T, 60.4 GB, Ubuntu 24.04), ZoneTree finished the full live insert/read/index-scan/query/update workload in 181,390 ms. RocksDB 6.2.2 via RocksDbSharp took 429,036 ms and SQLite 3.50.3 took 1,062,037 ms, all with identical checksums. Id reads ran 3.6x faster than RocksDB and email lookups 2.8x faster; raw inserts tied, and RocksDB led on insert-plus-stabilize readiness (154,360/s vs 141,281/s). At 100M profiles the read lead shrinks to about 1.9x and updates tie, and at 20M and 50M RocksDB wins the raw insert and update phases.
